title: Blue Monday, bunks, funerals and street advertising
summary: Monday was the big dance night; banquets with gumbo and fried chicken, funeral bands and trucks advertising dances on Sundays are described.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Did they have dances most nights or just one night a week?

Well people would hire a place, rent a place and give dances but the most nights they would have would be on a Monday night. Monday was a big dance night. They'd used to have bonkers on Mondays and in the daytime you know and picnics on Mondays.
How do you explain that on a Monday night when most people you know have things on weekend now they can go to work in the week. Yeah. They'd call it Blue Monday.
People wouldn't go to work. Some people wouldn't go to work on a Monday they'd call it Blue Monday.

It's like they have a, they just call them bonkers, the real name is a banquet you know, but they call them bonkers in them days. They'd have one at the economy hall maybe the neighbors playing. Chris Kelley might be playing at the cop raiders hall, another band somewhere else. Or sometimes we didn't have to go to school we'd make all of them. Yeah.
I mean. That's a pretty good idea. And that's why not bother about going to work on Monday.

Yeah. Well I mean you should have a fine time too. Like sometime on a weekday you'd be surprised they'd have two or three bands at one funeral. Or maybe two or three funerals and each funeral had a band. See the Catholicists have bands for their funerals too. I mean this was cut out in later years. But man you'd see a funeral passing here and you're looking at that funeral and you'd say, wait a minute how come another one now and I have a band. Yeah. That was a wonderful day for music. I don't know it just time went by but this was so different. I don't know everything was, in fact it was better than me. You know what I mean? I mean on a Sunday, all right, now it's around here sometime now on a Sunday's day, you know that. Unless they got some little parade or some activity going on. While on a Sunday you could look forward on a Sunday to see three or four advertisements, you know, and see the truck back up against one another bucking on the corner, see what band was going to pull away a force, you know. Well that was fun. So then you say, oh H&O's, so it's advertising too. They're going to come down there and then you go down there and wait for them. Yeah, I mean that was fun. Then the gang of kids would be following on their skates, you know roller skates. Yeah, that was fun. I enjoyed that.
Well these bunkays or whatever you call it, was that at night time? During the day, during the day.

During the day in the morning, eight, nine, ten o'clock like that in the morning. Some of them start twelve o'clock, you know, some maybe one to five like that. That'd be in the middle of the day. They'd have music while they ate or when they do it? Well they had food there to eat, eat and dance and band play and usually have a table set for the band and the intermission of the band go out there and eat gumbo and you know, whatever they have there. Oh yeah, that was...
We went to one of the union bunkays, I guess they called that about two years ago. Yeah. Was it something like that now? No, no. Or is that all different?
Well yeah, it's different. Well I mean the union was with that fried chicken. Fried chicken, you'd go up there and help yourself.
But did they serve the tangles those days?

Yeah, in those days if they'd have sandwiches they'd have lined up all on the table and any place you'd go now to a banquet in them days they'd have twice as much. Yeah. You know? Then they'd be serving hot gumbo, red beans and rice and all things like that. You'd get them hungry.
Yeah. Yeah. That'd make you hungry.
